questions.solution_text:
$f(x) = \sin x$, so $f'(x) = \cos x$.
$\int\cos x\left(\sin x\right)^{6}dx$
$= \dfrac{\sin^{7}x}{7} + C$

options.why: Missed that $f'(x) = -\sin x$ for the inner function $\cos x$, so the minus sign was dropped.
Raised the factor $\sin x$ to the new power instead of the inner function $\cos x$.
Raised the wrong function to the new power and also dropped the minus sign coming from $f'(x) = -\sin x$.

questions.solution_text:
$f(x) = \cos x$, so $f'(x) = -\sin x$.
$\int\sin x\left(\cos x\right)^{3}dx$
$= -\int -\sin x\left(\cos x\right)^{3}dx$
$= -\dfrac{\cos^{4}x}{4} + C$

options.why: Dropped the minus sign coming from $f'(x) = -\sin x$, giving $\left[\dfrac{\cos^{3}x}{3}\right]_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}$.
Substituted only the upper limit, where $\cos\dfrac{\pi}{2} = 0$, and never subtracted the value at the lower limit.
Divided by $2$, the original index, instead of by $3$, the new index.
Multiplied by $5$ instead of dividing by it to undo the $5$ the chain rule produces.
Raised the factor $\sec^{2}x$ to the new power instead of the inner function $\tan x$.
Raised the wrong function to the new power and multiplied by $5$ instead of dividing by it.

questions.question_text: Which one of these integrals **cannot** be found by the reverse chain rule as it stands?

options.why: The factor $x^{2}$ is a constant multiple of $f'(x) = 3x^{2}$, so the method works after taking $\dfrac{1}{3}$ outside.
The factor $6x^{5}$ is exactly $f'(x)$ for the inner function $x^{6}$, so the method applies directly.
The inner function is $\sin x$ and its derivative $\cos x$ is present as a factor, so the method applies.

questions.solution_text:
For $\int\cos\left(x^{3}\right)dx$ the inner function is $x^{3}$, so $f'(x) = 3x^{2}$.
The integrand contains no factor of $x^{2}$, and a missing factor cannot be created by moving a constant outside.
$\int\cos\left(x^{3}\right)dx$ cannot be found by the reverse chain rule.
